title: How Ohio’s brand-new advanced math policy will work https://fordhaminstitute.org/ohio/commentary/how-ohios-brand-new-advanced-math-policy-will-work
author: Aaron Churchill
summary: Aaron Churchill explains Ohio's new Senate Bill 19, which automatically enrolls high-achieving math students in advanced learning the following year, with the aim that all high achievers can complete Algebra I by eighth grade. Eligibility rests on state test scores, with students scoring advanced qualifying automatically and those scoring accomplished needing an A or B or a diagnostic score. He walks through what advancement looks like from fourth to sixth grade, where schools must offer either above-grade-level courses or vaguer services and curriculum modifications, and then the seventh and eighth grade compacted course leading to Algebra I. He praises the early start and objective criteria but warns that the flexible elementary option could produce uneven or low-quality programs. He concludes that implementation, especially for middle schools that must overhaul their offerings, will decide whether the framework delivers.
points: Ohio now joins North Carolina and Texas in automatic-enrollment math policies tied to state test results, which makes identification objective and universal rather than dependent on subjective referral.

About half of third and fourth graders would qualify, but only about one in three sixth graders, which would still sharply raise the share taking Algebra I by eighth grade from the current 20 percent.
The elementary option of vague services or curriculum modifications risks sporadic enrichment or lackluster online modules, while above-grade-level placement builds rigor into daily coursework.
Sixth grade is the pivotal year, because qualifying students move into a compacted seventh and eighth grade course that leads to Algebra I.
Schools without existing compacted courses must overhaul their middle school programs, and state officials should monitor implementation and collect data on gaps.
quotes: Education systems often fail to challenge our very brightest students. The unfortunate result is that too many high achievers lose their edge and fall short of their potential.

The link to state assessment results is critical: The tests are taken universally, so high-achievers from all backgrounds can be identified. It also means that math advancement decisions are based on objective standards (accomplished and advanced indicate being on-track for college) rather than subjective judgments alone.

Ohio rightly calls for early action, with advancement starting in fourth grade based on third-grade scores. Although the two service options outlined above provide districts with flexibility, they could also result in uneven advancement opportunities for students.
The “services or curricula modifications” option, on the other hand, is just vague enough to open the door for lower-quality programs (e.g., sporadic “enrichment” or lackluster online modules).

Moving forward, state officials should monitor how elementary schools implement “advanced learning opportunities,” which should include collecting data to help identify gaps in the types of opportunities elementary students receive.
Schools that have not offered compacted math courses, on the other hand, will need to overhaul their middle school programs.
Ohio lawmakers have established an admirable advanced math framework. Now it’s time to start the work of implementing these policies well.
